objects: GWAS SNPs; functional categories; genome-wide SNP-heritability; LD
assumptions: Complex-trait GWAS with heritability outside genome-wide significant loci
conclusion: The method aims to estimate functional-category proportions of genome-wide SNP-heritability using all SNPs while explicitly accounting for LD.
scope: Motivation for genome-wide functional partitioning, rather than restriction to significant loci
span: In GWAS of complex traits, much of the heritability lies in single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that do not reach genome-wide significance at current sample sizes [1, 2]. However, many current approaches that leverage functional information [3, 4] and GWAS data to inform disease biology use only SNPs in genome-wide significant loci [5–8], assume only one causal SNP per locus [9], or do not account for linkage disequilibrium (LD) [10]. We aim to improve power by estimating the proportion of genome-wide SNP-heritability [1] attributable to various functional categories, using information from all SNPs and explicitly modeling LD.

conclusion: The quantitative phenotype is modeled as the sum of standardized-genotype effects and mean-zero noise.

span: We assume a linear model: y_{i} = ∑ j X_{i j} β_{j} + ε_{i} where yi is a quantitative phenotype in individual i, Xij is the standardized genotype of individual i at the j-th SNP, βj is the effect size of SNP j, and εi is mean-zero noise.

span: We model β as a mean-zero random vector with independent entries. objects: Per-normalized-genotype effects; functional annotations; allele frequency p
assumptions: Conditioning on functional annotation; allele-frequency bins omitted from the annotations for the implied scaling
conclusion: Effects are assumed iid and mean zero conditional on annotation, implying per-allele effect variance proportional to 1/[p(1-p)] when allele-frequency bins are omitted.
scope: Stated conditional effect assumption and its allele-frequency implication
span: Stratified LD score regression is based on the assumption that the per-normalized-genotype effect size of a SNP is drawn i.i.d. with mean zero, conditioned on functional annotation. So if allele frequency bins are not included as annotations in the model, then we are assuming that per-allele effect sizes have variance proportional to (p(1−p))−1 for allele frequency p.

span: Here, we introduce a method for partitioning heritability, stratified LD score regression, that requires only GWAS summary statistics and LD information from an external reference panel that matches the population studied in the GWAS.

objects: REML-based heritability partitioning; individual-level genotypes; summary statistics
assumptions: Large GWAS meta-analyses or multiple functional categories at sample sizes in the tens of thousands
conclusion: The authors motivate stratified LD score regression by contrasting it with REML partitioning, which requires individual genotypes and becomes computationally intractable for many categories at large sample sizes.
scope: Stated input and computational contrast; no estimator-equivalence assertion
span: Previous work on partitioning SNP-heritability has used restricted maximum likelihood (REML) as implemented in GCTA [1, 11–14]. REML requires individual genotypes, but many of the largest GWAS analyses are conducted through meta-analysis of study-specific results, and so typically only summary statistics, not individual genotypes, are available for these studies. Even when individual genotypes are available, using REML to analyze multiple functional categories becomes computationally intractable at sample sizes in the tens of thousands.

objects: Trait polygenicity; sample size; SNP-heritability; LD reference population; custom genotyping arrays
assumptions: Reasonable power and accurate external-reference analysis
conclusion: The method needs sufficient sample size or SNP-heritability and polygenicity, requires a population-matched LD reference for accuracy, and is not currently applicable to custom-array studies.
scope: Three author-stated operating limits; European datasets and 1000G European reference used in this paper
span: First, for the method to have reasonable power, the dataset analyzed must have a very large sample size and/or large SNP-heritability, and the trait analyzed must be polygenic (Figure 1). Second, the method requires an LD reference panel matched to the population studied to give accurate results; all results here are from European datasets and use 1000G Europeans as a reference panel (see Online Methods and Supplementary Figure 4). Third, our method is currently not applicable to studies using custom genotyping arrays (e.g., Metabochip; see Supplementary Note).

objects: Additive SNP contributions; reference-panel SNPs; available cell-type annotations; small functional categories
assumptions: Application of the additive reference-panel-based functional enrichment method
conclusion: The method omits non-additive effects and causal SNPs outside the reference panel, cannot detect enrichment in unmeasured cell types, and has large standard errors for very small categories.
scope: Three author-stated scope and precision limits; extremely rare-variant enrichment may differ
span: Fourth, our method is based on an additive model and does not consider the contribution of epistatic or other non-additive effects, nor does it model causal contributions of SNPs not in the reference panel; in particular, it is possible that patterns of enrichment at extremely rare variants may be different from those inferred using this method (see Online Methods). Fifth, the method is limited by available functional data: if a trait is enriched in a cell type for which we have no data, we cannot detect the enrichment. Sixth, our method currently gives large standard errors when applied to very small categories (Supplementary Figure 8 and Supplementary Note).

objects: Unidentified functional categories; misspecified annotation model; enrichment estimates
assumptions: True enrichment occurs in a functional category omitted from the model
conclusion: The authors cannot rule out enrichment-estimation bias from model misspecification caused by an unidentified functional category.
scope: General robustness is not guaranteed by the reported simulations
span: Last, though we have shown our method to be robust in a wide range of scenarios, we cannot rule out bias due to model misspecification caused by enrichment in an unidentified functional category as a possible source of bias; however our simulations show that our method gives nearly unbiased results even under very extreme scenarios of unmodeled functional categories (Figure 2).

objects: SNP universe; category collection C_c; all-SNP category
conclusion: Every SNP must belong to at least one modeled category, achieved by a disjoint genome partition or inclusion of an all-SNP category.
scope: Coverage assumption; the categories themselves are selected modeling settings
span: Each SNP must be in at least one category; in practice we either have a set of categories that forms a disjoint partition of the genome, or we include the set of all SNPs as one of the categories.
